tagline: A Persian court official's own account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, renewing the covenant under the law of Moses, and fighting to keep a restored people faithful.
overview:
Nehemiah was a Jew serving as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I in the royal city of Susa. In 445 BC he hears that the walls of Jerusalem still lie broken and its gates burned, nearly a century after the first exiles came home. He prays, risks his position by asking the king for leave, and comes to Jerusalem as governor. Against mockery, threats, and plots from neighboring officials, he organizes the people to rebuild the whole circuit of the wall, and it is finished in fifty-two days (6:15).

The wall is only the first half of the book. Once the city is secure, Ezra reads the law of Moses to the assembled people (chapter 8), the people confess their sins in a long prayer that retells Israel's history (chapter 9), and they sign a binding agreement to keep the law (chapter 10). Nehemiah then repopulates the thinly settled city, and the wall is dedicated with two great choirs processing on top of it. The book ends with Nehemiah returning after an absence to find the people slipping back into the very failings they had promised to avoid, and dealing with them sharply.

Nehemiah is one of the most personal books of the Old Testament. Much of it is his own memoir, full of quick prayers, strong feelings, and honest self-defense. It shows a layman in government work who treats prayer and planning as partners, and it shows a community learning that walls, however necessary, cannot by themselves make a people faithful.
author:
Large parts of the book are written in the first person by Nehemiah himself (1:1 to 7:5, the dedication of the wall in 12:27-43, and most of chapter 13). This material is usually called the Nehemiah Memoir, and most scholars, whatever their other views, accept it as substantially his. Its style, with short prayers asking God to remember him (5:19, 13:14, 13:31), is distinctive. The rest of the book, including the list of returnees in chapter 7 (which repeats Ezra 2), the account of Ezra's reading of the law in chapters 8 to 10, and the lists of chapters 11 and 12, comes from other sources.

In the Hebrew tradition Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, and the same compiler shaped both. Jewish tradition in the Talmud credits Ezra with writing the book and Nehemiah with completing it. Modern scholars debate whether the compiler also wrote Chronicles; many now think Ezra-Nehemiah is a separate work, while others still see a close link. The book was later divided, and in some older Christian Bibles Nehemiah was called Second Esdras.
date:
The events are unusually well dated. Nehemiah receives the news in the month of Chislev in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (1:1) and speaks to the king in Nisan of that year (2:1). With Artaxerxes I, who reigned 465-424 BC, this places Nehemiah's arrival in Jerusalem in 445 BC. He served as governor for twelve years, until the king's thirty-second year, 433 BC (5:14, 13:6), then returned to the king and came back to Jerusalem some time later. The Elephantine papyri, letters from a Jewish community in southern Egypt dated about 407 BC, mention the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, and a high priest named Johanan in Jerusalem, which fits the setting of Nehemiah well.

The relative order of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated (see the introduction to Ezra), since Nehemiah 8 and 12 show them together. The book in its final form, with priestly lists running to Jaddua (12:11, 22), probably dates from around 400 BC or somewhat later.
setting:
Nehemiah lives at the heart of the Persian Empire. Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran, was one of the royal capitals, and a cupbearer served the king his wine and was expected to be utterly trustworthy, which gave him rare access to the king. Judah (Yehud) was a small province within the satrapy Beyond the River, west of the Euphrates. Jerusalem itself was thinly populated, and its walls had lain in ruins since the Babylonians broke them down in 587 or 586 BC. An earlier attempt to rebuild them had been stopped by royal order (Ezra 4:7-23).

The neighbors were powerful and wary. Sanballat the Horonite was governor of Samaria to the north. Tobiah, the Ammonite official, had influence east of the Jordan and ties by marriage to leading families in Jerusalem. Geshem the Arab probably represents the Arab kingdom of Qedar to the south; a silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt names a Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, whom many identify as Geshem's son. Inside Judah, the people faced heavy taxes, debt, and poor harvests, and some were selling their children into servitude (chapter 5).
purpose: The book was written for the post-exilic community to show how God restored Jerusalem as a city and its people as a covenant community, and to call that community to lasting faithfulness. It holds up Nehemiah as an example of prayerful, courageous leadership, and it presents the reading of the law and the renewal of the covenant as the true center of the restoration. Its unresolved ending is part of its purpose: it warns that promises made in a great assembly must be kept in ordinary weeks, in the matters of the Sabbath, the temple's upkeep, and marriage.
story: Nehemiah continues the story told in Ezra. The first exiles returned under Cyrus in 538 BC and finished the temple in 515 BC; Ezra came with a second group in 458 BC (on the traditional dating). About thirteen years later Nehemiah arrives to rebuild the city walls. His book is the last historical narrative of the Old Testament, and the prophet Malachi, who confronts many of the same problems (careless priests, neglected tithes, broken marriages), probably spoke in the same general period. After Nehemiah the Old Testament story falls silent until the New Testament opens in a Jerusalem ruled by Rome, whose temple and walls descend, through later rebuilding, from the work of these years.
christ: Nehemiah shows a restored city that is still waiting. The walls are rebuilt, the law is read, and the covenant is renewed, yet in the great prayer of chapter 9 the people say that they are slaves in their own land, with foreign kings ruling over them. The book ends with Nehemiah asking God to remember him, not with a kingdom established. The Old Testament's longing for a true restoration, a new covenant written on the heart and a king who would build God's house forever, remains open. The New Testament finds that longing met in Jesus, who weeps over Jerusalem, cleanses its temple, and brings a covenant in which the law is written on hearts. The links here are mostly thematic: Nehemiah's intercession for his people, his costly leaving of the palace for a ruined city, and his zeal for God's house are patterns the Gospels fill with greater meaning, not predictions the book makes.
reading: Read Nehemiah as a memoir set inside a larger historical book. Listen for Nehemiah's voice: his quick prayers in the middle of action (2:4), his lament, his anger, and his repeated appeals to God to remember him. Don't skip the lists of builders, returnees, and signers, which record the names of ordinary people who did the work. Notice how the book turns at chapter 8 from building the city to building the people, and that the high point is not the wall's completion but the reading of the law. Finally, read the harsh measures of chapter 13 with care. The book presents Nehemiah as sincere and largely in the right, but it also lets the reader see a reform that must be enforced again and again, which is part of its message.

structure.title: Nehemiah's burden and commission
structure.summary: In Susa Nehemiah hears of Jerusalem's ruin, prays, asks Artaxerxes for leave, and arrives in Jerusalem, where he inspects the walls by night and calls the people to build.

structure.title: The wall rebuilt against opposition
structure.summary: Families and groups rebuild the wall section by section, while Nehemiah faces mockery, threats of attack, economic injustice among the Jews themselves, and plots against his life. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and Nehemiah turns to the city's population, using the list of the first returnees.

structure.title: The law read and the covenant renewed
structure.summary: Ezra reads the law to the assembled people, who celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, confess their sins in a great prayer, and sign a binding agreement to keep God's commands.

structure.title: A city peopled and a wall dedicated
structure.summary: One in ten of the people move into Jerusalem, the lists of priests and Levites are recorded, and the wall is dedicated with processions and great joy.

structure.title: Nehemiah's final reforms
structure.summary: Returning after an absence, Nehemiah expels Tobiah from a temple chamber, restores support for the Levites, enforces the Sabbath, and confronts marriages outside the covenant.

themes.title: Prayer and action together
themes.body: Nehemiah prays at length when he hears the news (chapter 1), prays in a single breath before answering the king (2:4), and sets guards while praying against attack. The book never sets prayer against planning. It treats careful work, risk, and organization as ways of trusting God.

themes.title: The people of God rebuilt
themes.body: The wall is rebuilt by dozens of families, guilds, and towns, each at its own section, and the book records their names. Restoration is a shared work. The same book insists that a people is rebuilt not only by stones but by hearing God's word, confessing sin, and binding themselves to obey.

themes.title: Opposition from without and within
themes.body: Enemies mock, threaten, and scheme, and some of the danger comes from inside: nobles who exploit the poor, prophets hired to frighten Nehemiah, and a priest who gave Tobiah a room in the temple. The book is honest that the community's worst threats are sometimes its own members.

themes.title: Justice for the poor
themes.body: In chapter 5 Nehemiah stops the building to confront Jews who were charging interest to their own brothers and taking their fields and children for debts. He cancels the debts and refuses the governor's food allowance. For this book, a rebuilt city with an unjust economy is not a restored city.

themes.title: Covenant faithfulness in ordinary life
themes.body: The covenant of chapter 10 is concrete: marriage, the Sabbath, the temple tax, firstfruits, and tithes. Chapter 13 shows those very commitments failing. Faithfulness, in Nehemiah, is measured in markets, storerooms, and households, and it has to be renewed.

keyChapters.why: Nehemiah's prayer of confession, grounded in God's covenant promises to Moses, shows how the book's action begins in intercession.
Nehemiah risks his post before the king, receives leave to rebuild, and calls the people of Jerusalem to begin the work.
Nehemiah halts the project to confront the exploitation of poor Jews by their own nobles, showing that justice belongs to rebuilding.
Ezra reads the law to the whole people, the Levites explain it, and the people's weeping turns to joy in the Feast of Tabernacles.
A great prayer retells Israel's history as a story of God's faithfulness and the people's rebellion, and admits they are still slaves in their own land.
The book ends not in triumph but with renewed failure and renewed reform, and with Nehemiah asking God to remember him.
